Operator: Good day, and welcome to the Global Asset Partners Q3 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants are in a listen-only mode. After the speakers' presentation, there will be a question and answer session. As a reminder, during the presentation, the listen-only mode will be in effect. To ask a question during the Q&A, please press star then one on your touchtone phone. To withdraw your question, press star then two. Please be advised that today's conference is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the call over to Emily Carter, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Emily Carter: Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining us today to discuss Global Asset Partners' Q3 2024 results. Joining me on today's call are John Reynolds, Chief Executive Officer; Sarah Thompson, Chief Financial Officer; Michael Chen, Chief Investment Officer; Lisa Patel, Head of Distribution; and David Wong, Head of Operations.

Before we begin, I'd like to remind you that some of the statements made today may be forward-looking. Please refer to our SEC filings for a discussion of the risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially.

With that, I'll turn the call over to John Reynolds.

John Reynolds: Thank you, Emily, and good morning, everyone. Thank you for joining us. I'm pleased to report on our performance for Q3. We achieved solid results this quarter, driven by strong net inflows, top-decile fund performance, and disciplined capital management. Our AUM grew to $1.25 trillion.

Sarah Thompson: Thank you, John. From a financial perspective, Global Asset Partners delivered strong results in Q3. Our revenue was $1.42 billion, representing a 12% increase year-over-year. This growth was primarily driven by higher average AUM from both market appreciation and robust net inflows, alongside a favorable mix shift toward higher-fee alternatives and performance fees. Our expenses were $920 million, resulting in net income of $485 million. Our expense ratio improved to 18 basis points due to operating leverage from AUM scale and efficiencies in technology deployment.

Now, turning to our net flows, which remain a cornerstone of our organic growth story here at Global Asset Partners. For the third quarter, we delivered net inflows of $14.2 billion, bringing year-to-date net inflows to $42.8 billion—a robust 28% increase over the prior-year period. This performance not only outpaced the industry average of 12% as reported by Morningstar Direct but also positions us favorably against peers like BlackRock and T. Rowe Price, where industry-wide flows have been tempered by selective rotation out of mega-cap tech into value and small-cap strategies.

Let me break this down by the key drivers, starting with fund performance, which continues to be our most potent magnet for inflows. Our active equity strategies generated $8.7 billion in net new money during the quarter, accounting for 61% of total inflows. This was propelled by top-decile performance across several flagship products. For instance, our Global Asset Partners U.S. Large-Cap Growth Fund benefited from overweight positions in AI-driven leaders like NVIDIA and Broadcom amid the ongoing generative AI hype cycle, delivering a 1-year return of 42.3% as of quarter-end, ranking in the top 5% of its Lipper peer group. Similarly, our International Equity Fund captured $2.1 billion in flows, up 35% quarter-over-quarter, thanks to alpha generation from selective exposure to European industrials and Japanese exporters, which returned 18.7% over the trailing 12 months—outperforming the MSCI EAFE Index by 450 basis points.

On the fixed income side, we saw $3.9 billion in inflows, or 27% of the total, driven by our short-duration and investment-grade strategies amid persistent Fed signaling on rate cuts. The Global Asset Partners Core Bond Fund attracted $1.8 billion alone, with its 4.2% yield-to-worst and a duration of just 2.8 years resonating with yield-hungry institutional clients reallocating from cash equivalents. Performance here was stellar, with 92% of our fixed income AUM beating its benchmark on a 3-year annualized basis, per Morningstar ratings—four stars across the board for most strategies. This outperformance stems from our proprietary yield curve modeling, which anticipated the September Fed pivot and allowed us to ladder into high-quality corporates ahead of the curve.

Market trends have been equally supportive, though not without headwinds. The broader equity rally, with the S&P 500 up 22% YTD and the Nasdaq Composite gaining 28%, created a favorable tide for our growth-oriented products. However, we've navigated rotation risks adeptly: as investors shifted from the "Magnificent Seven" megacaps—now trading at 32x forward earnings—into our small- and mid-cap value funds, we captured $1.4 billion in those sleeves. Net flows into small caps surged 45% QoQ for us, aligning with the Russell 2000's 15% rebound post-election uncertainty.

In alternatives, a bright spot amid volatile public markets, we posted $1.6 billion in inflows, led by our private credit and infrastructure strategies. With global dry powder in private markets exceeding $2.5 trillion per Preqin data, clients are flocking to our Global Asset Partners Direct Lending Fund, which offers a targeted 9.8% net IRR with low correlation to equities (beta of 0.12). This reflects a secular trend: alternatives now comprise 22% of our $1.25 trillion AUM, up from 15% two years ago, as pensions and sovereign wealth funds seek illiquidity premia in a higher-for-longer rate environment.

Regionally, our flows tell a nuanced story. In the U.S., which drove 55% of Q3 inflows at $7.8 billion, retail investors via our ETF suite—particularly the Global Asset Partners ESG Equity ETF (ESGX), with $900 million in creations—poured in amid record 401(k) contributions, up 11% YoY per ICI data. Institutional DC plans favored our target-date funds, adding $2.2 billion as glide paths adjusted for longer horizons.

Europe contributed 25% of flows, or $3.6 billion, bolstered by MiFID II-compliant transparency and our UCITS-compliant products. The Euro Stoxx 50's 14% gain fueled equity inflows, but fixed income dominated as ECB rate cuts to 3.25% prompted a $1.5 billion shift into our Euro Aggregate Bond Fund. We've gained share here through partnerships with platforms like Allfunds, where our funds now rank in the top quartile for flows.

Asia-Pacific was our fastest-growing region at 18% of inflows ($2.6 billion), with strong demand from HNWIs in Greater China and Southeast Asia. Our Global Asset Partners Asia ex-Japan Equity Fund scooped $800 million, riding the Nikkei 225's surge to 40,000 amid Abenomics 2.0 and yen weakening. However, outflows from China-focused mandates—$200 million—highlighted geopolitical tensions, which we're mitigating via tactical underweights and pivots to India and Vietnam growth stories.

Technical initiatives have amplified these organic drivers. Our recent launch of the Global Asset Partners Flow Optimizer platform—a proprietary API-driven tool integrating Aladdin-like risk analytics with real-time flow forecasting—has boosted advisor retention by 15%, enabling personalized sleeve recommendations that increased average client ticket sizes by 22%. We've also expanded distribution via model portfolio marketplaces like Envestnet and Orion, driving $4.1 billion in SMA inflows YTD. On the tech front, our AI-enhanced portfolio construction engine, leveraging machine learning on alternative data sets like satellite imagery for supply chain alpha, has improved our hit rate on stock picks by 18%, directly correlating to higher Lipper rankings and flows.

Strategically, we're laser-focused on long-term flow sustainability. Client retention hit 96% this quarter, with churn below 1% in core strategies, thanks to our "sticky" multi-asset solutions like the Global Asset Partners Balanced Allocation Fund, which saw $1.2 billion in rebalancing flows. We're doubling down on thematic investing—launching three new ETFs in Q4: one on AI infrastructure, one on energy transition, and a climate-resilient credit fund—targeting the $500 billion ESG flow opportunity projected by BloombergNEF. Institutional wins include a $5 billion mandate from a CalPERS-like pension, emphasizing our scalable OCIO model.

That said, risks loom: potential U.S. fiscal policy shifts post-election could pressure duration-sensitive flows, and if the VIX spikes above 25 on recession fears, we might see tactical outflows into money markets—currently at 18% of industry AUM per EPFR. But our positioning is resilient: 65% of AUM in active strategies with proven downside capture ratios below 90%, and a deliberate underweight to high-beta cyclicals.

These net flows underscore our competitive moat in performance, product innovation, and client-centric tech. With AUM now at $1.25 trillion, up 16% YoY, we're well-set for 2025.

Good afternoon, everyone. Today, I'd like to dive into our performance fees realized and how our strategies have performed against key benchmarks—a critical driver of our revenue mix and a testament to our active management edge. As you know, performance fees, which typically represent 20% of profits above a high-water mark or hurdle rate—often the 3-month LIBOR plus 500 basis points for our hedge funds—crystallize quarterly or annually depending on the mandate. In Q3, we realized $178 million in performance fees across our flagship strategies, up 32% year-over-year from $135 million in Q3 2023. This surge was fueled by strong alpha generation in our equity long/short and credit opportunistic sleeves, amid a resilient U.S. equity market and selective outperformance in fixed income despite persistent rate volatility.

Let me break this down by asset class, with a focus on our relative performance versus benchmarks like the S&P 500 for U.S. large-cap equities, the Bloomberg Barclays U.S. Aggregate Bond Index (BB Agg) for core fixed income, the MSCI EAFE for developed international equities, and the MSCI Emerging Markets Index for EM exposure. Our total AUM stood at $1.25 trillion at quarter-end, with $780 billion in fee-generating strategies, of which 28% are now performance-linked—up from 24% a year ago, reflecting client demand for skin-in-the-game alignment.

Our U.S. equity composites delivered a net return of 8.2% in Q3, outperforming the S&P 500's 7.9% gain by 30 basis points on an asset-weighted basis. Annualized over the trailing three years, we're ahead by 2.4 percentage points, with an information ratio of 0.65—well above our peer median of 0.42 per Morningstar data. Key drivers included our Global Asset Partners Large Cap Growth Fund (AUM: $42 billion), which returned 9.1% versus the Russell 1000 Growth's 8.4%, benefiting from overweight positions in AI enablers like NVIDIA and Broadcom ahead of the earnings cycle. We realized $92 million in performance fees here, crystallizing on 15% of AUM crossing high-water marks.

Internationally, our EAFE strategies returned 5.6% net, edging the MSCI EAFE by 110 basis points, driven by tactical underweights in cyclically exposed Japanese autos and tactical overs in defensive Swiss healthcare names like Roche. In EM, we navigated a choppy 4.1% return for the MSCI EM Index with a 5.3% composite gain—alpha of 120 bps—via our China A-share active extension sleeve, which captured re-rating in consumer staples amid policy easing signals from Beijing.

Regionally, U.S. equities contributed 62% of our equity performance fees, Europe 22%, and Asia-Pac/EM 16%. A technical initiative worth noting is our deployment of machine learning-enhanced factor models in our quant equity pods, which improved our momentum and quality factor tilts, boosting Sharpe ratios by 15% quarter-over-quarter.

In a quarter marked by the Fed's signaling and sticky 3.5% core PCE inflation, our core fixed income strategies returned 1.8% net, outperforming the BB Agg's 0.9% by 90 basis points. Over three years, we're up 1.2% annualized, with duration management key: we de-risked to 5.8 years from 6.4 at year-start, rotating into short-duration investment-grade corporates and agency MBS. Our Global Asset Partners Total Return Bond Fund (AUM: $28 billion) led with a 2.3% return, realizing $41 million in fees on its 10% hurdle.

High-yield and opportunistic credit shone brighter, returning 3.4% versus the ICE BofA High Yield Index's 2.7%, with $45 million in fees from CCC-rated energy refiners like Valero, positioned for OPEC+ cuts. We've integrated ESG overlays here, excluding 12% of the universe on thermal coal exposure, which enhanced risk-adjusted returns with a tracking error under 2.5%.

Our alternatives platform, including our Global Asset Partners Meridian Hedge Fund (AUM: $65 billion), posted 4.7% net—well clear of its cash + 400 bps hurdle—versus the HFRI Fund Weighted Composite's 3.2%. This unlocked $68 million in fees, with event-driven catalysts in M&A (e.g., activist stakes in legacy media like Paramount) and macro trades shorting European sovereigns amid fiscal divergence. Private markets saw $12 million in carried interest realizations from two secondary exits in North American mid-market PE, with IRRs of 22% and 19% versus the Cambridge Associates benchmark.

These results underscore our disciplined approach: 72% of our strategies beat benchmarks over one year, 81% over three, and 88% over five—superior to the 60/75/80 industry averages per eVestment. Client flows reflect this: $14.2 billion in net inflows, 40% into performance-fee vehicles. Looking forward, we're positioning for a soft-landing scenario with tactical equity overweight in U.S. small-cap value (Russell 2000 Value) and fixed income extension into EM local currency debt, targeting 150-200 bps of pick-up over U.S. Treasuries. Our quant initiatives, including NLP sentiment analysis on 10-K filings, are scaling to $100 billion AUM by year-end, enhancing alpha persistence.

Good afternoon, everyone. As we review our financial performance, I'd like to dive into our operating expenses, which totaled $452 million for the quarter, representing a modest 4.2% year-over-year increase. This came in slightly ahead of our guided range but reflects disciplined cost management amid a challenging macro environment, including persistent inflation pressures and elevated regulatory scrutiny across our key markets.

To contextualize, our operating expense ratio—defined as total OpEx as a percentage of average AUM—improved to 18 basis points from 19 bps in Q3 2023, driven by AUM growth to $1.25 trillion, up 12% YoY, fueled by net inflows of $18 billion, particularly into our low-fee ETF suites and private markets strategies. This efficiency underscores our focus on scale, where fixed costs are increasingly leveraged across a broader asset base. Sequential to Q2 2024, OpEx rose 2.1%, primarily from seasonal compensation accruals, but we remain on track for full-year OpEx growth of 4-6%, below revenue growth projections of 9-11%.

Let me break this down by category, with year-over-year comparisons and key drivers:

Compensation and Benefits: $248 million, or 55% of total OpEx, up 3.1% YoY. This remains our largest line item, consistent with industry peers like BlackRock and T. Rowe Price, where talent drives alpha generation. The increase was driven by a 2.5% rise in base salaries to support retention in a competitive talent market—our voluntary turnover rate held steady at 8%, below the industry average of 12% per Greenwich Associates data. Variable comp, including performance bonuses tied to our long-term incentive plan, accounted for $85 million, or 34% of the category. Payouts were moderated versus last year due to softer fixed income performance amid higher-for-longer rates, but we front-loaded equity grants in high-conviction areas like our Global Asset Partners ESG Equity Fund, which saw $4.2 billion in inflows. Regionally, EMEA comp costs grew 7% due to hiring portfolio managers for our UCITS-compliant strategies, while APAC remained flat as we optimized our Singapore hub post the 2023 restructuring.

Distribution, Servicing, and Marketing: $102 million, or 23% of total OpEx, up 8.7% YoY. This category reflects sub-advisory fees, 12b-1 payments, and marketing spend to capture retail and RIA flows. The uptick was propelled by $2.8 billion in ETF inflows, necessitating higher platform fees to partners like Schwab and Fidelity, mirroring industry trends where ETFs now comprise 28% of our AUM, akin to Vanguard's dominance. Servicing costs for our model delivery group rose 5%, supporting advisor platforms amid the shift to direct indexing—a $1.1 billion AUM segment growing 25% YoY. Marketing initiatives, including digital campaigns for our Global Asset Partners Crypto-Linked ETF (launched Q4 2023, now $750 million AUM), added $12 million, with strong ROI as client acquisition costs fell 15% via targeted LinkedIn and advisor portal enhancements.

General and Administrative (G&A), including Occupancy: $58 million, or 13% of total OpEx, flat YoY. Strong cost control here, with a 2% reduction in occupancy expenses from subleasing our legacy New York office space post-hybrid work adoption—now at 60% utilization, aligning with peers like State Street Global Advisors. Professional fees ticked up 4% for audit and legal support around our SEC Rule 15c3-5 implementation for broker-dealer compliance, but we offset this with 10% savings in travel via virtual client roadshows. Regulatory tailwinds from the SEC's Private Fund Adviser rules added $3 million in one-offs, concentrated in our $45 billion alternatives platform.

Technology and Data Infrastructure: $28 million, or 6% of total OpEx, up 12% YoY. A strategic bright spot: We're accelerating capex-light tech investments, with $15 million allocated to cloud migration and AI enhancements to our proprietary risk analytics platform, Global Asset Partners Sentinel—inspired by BlackRock's Aladdin but tailored for mid-cap managers. This drove a 20% improvement in order management system efficiency, reducing trade execution costs by 8 bps. Data licensing for ESG and alternatives datasets (e.g., MSCI and Preqin feeds) rose 10%, critical for our $120 billion sustainable investing franchise amid EU SFDR reporting mandates. APAC tech spend grew 18% for blockchain integration in our tokenization pilots, positioning us ahead of the curve as Bitcoin ETFs like BlackRock's IBIT reshape the landscape.

Amortization, Depreciation, and Other: $16 million, or 3% of total OpEx, down 5% YoY. Primarily amortization of intangibles from our 2022 acquisition of Horizon Alternatives ($8 billion AUM add-on), now fully integrated. Depreciation on data centers declined as we shifted 70% of workloads to AWS, yielding $2 million in savings. Other includes minor provisions for credit losses on seed capital investments, negligible at $1.2 million.

Our OpEx profile reflects a deliberate shift toward a tech-enabled, variable-cost model, targeting a long-term expense ratio below 16 bps as AUM scales to $600 billion by 2026, but adjusted for our trajectory toward $1.5 trillion. Key initiatives include AI and Automation: Piloting generative AI for research summarization, projecting 15-20% comp productivity gains by FY2025, similar to Invesco's recent disclosures. Regional Optimization: Mitigating EMEA cost inflation via shared services from our Dublin hub, while APAC expansion focuses on fee-based revenue from sovereign wealth mandates. Efficiency Metrics: Our compensation-to-revenue ratio held at 42%, competitive with peers, and tech ROI is tracking at 3x via reduced front-office headcount needs. Risks include talent inflation if equity markets rally sharply, and potential regtech spend from evolving MiFID III rules. That said, our fortress balance sheet—with $1.2 billion in cash—provides ample dry powder for opportunistic M&A in high-margin SMAs.

Good afternoon, everyone. Before I hand it back, I'd like to dive deeper into the trends shaping our operating margin performance, which came in at 35.2% for the quarter—up 320 basis points year-over-year from 32.0% in Q3 2023, and 110 basis points sequentially from Q2's 34.1%. This marks our strongest quarterly margin in over two years and puts us on track for a full-year 2024 operating margin of 34% to 36%, ahead of our initial guidance.

Let me break this down by key drivers, starting with the top line. Our operating margin expansion was primarily fueled by robust revenue growth outpacing expense growth. Net revenues reached $1.42 billion in Q3, a 12% increase YoY, driven by average AUM of $1.25 trillion—up 14% from last year—benefiting from both market appreciation and $28 billion in net inflows, particularly into high-margin alternatives and ETFs. Fee rates held steady at 42 basis points overall, but we saw stabilization in our active equity strategies at 55 bps, even amid broader industry fee compression averaging 2-3 bps annually per Morningstar data.

On the expense side, our adjusted operating expenses rose only 7% YoY to $920 million, delivering meaningful operating leverage. Compensation and benefits, which comprise 45% of our opex, increased 6% to $415 million, moderated by a 2% headcount reduction in non-client-facing roles through targeted attrition and our 'Talent Optimization Program.' This included reallocating resources from legacy distribution teams to digital client acquisition channels, where we've seen ROI north of 5x.

A big tailwind here has been our technical initiatives around operational efficiency. We've accelerated our cloud migration to AWS, reducing IT infrastructure costs by 15% quarter-over-quarter, and rolled out our proprietary AI-driven 'Global Asset Partners AlphaForge' platform across our $450 billion active equity and multi-asset mandates. AlphaForge leverages machine learning for alpha generation and predictive risk modeling, cutting research costs by 18% while improving pre-tax returns by 120 bps in back-tested pilots against benchmarks like the MSCI World Index. This mirrors efficiencies seen at peers like BlackRock with their Aladdin platform, but we're applying it more aggressively to mid-market strategies.

Regionally, our margins vary meaningfully, reflecting product mix and regulatory dynamics. In the Americas, which represent 55% of AUM, margins expanded to 38%—our highest ever—thanks to scale in low-cost ETFs like our Global Asset Partners S&P 500 UCITS ETF, now at $120 billion AUM with 8 bps fees, and private credit funds yielding 12-15% IRRs amid higher rates. US net inflows of $18 billion were led by retirement channels, where 401(k) rollovers into our SMAs grew 25% YoY.

Europe, at 25% of AUM, saw margins at 32%, pressured by MiFID II unbundling but offset by 9% AUM growth to $450 billion, driven by ESG mandates—our Euro Stoxx 50 ESG ETF hit €15 billion AUM with 15 bps fees. We've invested €50 million in PRIIPs compliance tech, which should flow through as 50-100 bps margin accretion in 2025.

Asia-Pacific, our fastest-growing region at 20% of AUM and $360 billion, delivered 30% margins, up from 27% YoY, fueled by $7 billion inflows into China onshore equity funds and our Singapore-domiciled private markets platform targeting family offices. Here, strategic partnerships with local players like Temasek have lowered distribution costs by 20%, while regulatory tailwinds from Hong Kong's ETF Connect scheme are accelerating AUM beta.

Looking at longer-term trends, our operating margin has trended up from 28% five years ago, reflecting the compounding benefits of scale, product diversification, and tech investments.

Thank you, John, and good morning, everyone. I'll now turn to our client franchise, which remains the bedrock of Global Asset Partners'—or GAP's—long-term success. With $1.25 trillion in assets under management as of Q3 2024, up 12% year-over-year, our focus on client retention and disciplined new client acquisition has driven $22 billion in net new assets, or NNA, this quarter alone—exceeding our internal guidance by 8%. Let me break this down in detail, starting with retention, then acquisition, and wrap with our strategic initiatives amid a market backdrop of moderating inflation, Fed rate cuts, and persistent equity dispersion favoring active managers like us.

Our annualized client retention rate stands at an industry-leading 96.2% for the trailing 12 months, up 110 basis points from 95.1% in FY2023. This marks our 11th consecutive quarter above 95%, well ahead of the peer median of 92% as reported in the latest Greenwich Associates survey. For context, in a year where the S&P 500 returned 22% but fixed income benchmarks like the Bloomberg Aggregate lagged at just 1.2%, our ability to deliver alpha across mandates has been key.

Breaking it down by client segment: Institutional Clients (58% of AUM): Retention at 97.8%, bolstered by our $150 billion defined contribution and pension mandates. We retained 100% of our top-20 institutional relationships, including renewals with CalPERS and the New York State Common Retirement Fund, where our active equity strategies outperformed benchmarks by 250 bps net of fees. Intermediary/RIAs (32% of AUM): 95.5% retention, driven by our model delivery marketplace, which now supports 1,200 RIAs on platforms like Envestnet and Orion. Unified managed account, or UMA, sleeves grew 18% YoY, with low churn thanks to our tax-alpha overlays reducing client tax drag by an average 45 bps. High-Net-Worth Individuals (HNWIs) (10% of AUM): 93.4% retention, our strongest in three years, reflecting enhanced family office services amid wealth transfer dynamics—$84 trillion expected globally by 2045 per Cerulli Associates.

Regionally, Americas retention held firm at 96.8%, Europe dipped slightly to 94.2% due to MiFID II cost disclosure pressures but stabilized with our UCITS-compliant ETF suite, while APAC surged to 97.1% on inflows from sovereign wealth funds in Singapore and the Middle East, where our Sharia-compliant strategies captured 15% market share in sustainable Sukuk.

What’s driving this? First, performance: 78% of our composite strategies beat their benchmarks over three years, per Morningstar data, particularly in small-cap value and emerging markets debt. Second, technology: Our Client360 portal, powered by AI-driven predictive analytics, has reduced service tickets by 32% and enabled proactive rebalancing alerts, boosting net promoter scores to 82 from 76 a year ago. Third, stickiness from alternatives: Private credit and direct indexing AUM grew 25% YoY, with retention at 98%, as clients lock in illiquid premiums amid high yields.

On acquisition, we onboarded 1,450 net new clients this quarter, a 14% YoY increase, translating to that $22 billion NNA—$14 billion organic, $8 billion from two small RIA practice acquisitions totaling $5 billion AUM. This caps a nine-quarter streak of positive flows, contrasting with the $100 billion industry outflows in passive ETFs YTD, per EPFR data, as investors rotate to active amid volatility.

Pipeline conversion hit 42%, up from 38%, fueled by: Product Innovation: Launch of our GAP Horizon ESG Multi-Asset ETF (ESGZ), which gathered $3.2 billion since May inception, ranking #3 in its category per ETF.com. It appeals to RIAs seeking Article 8 SFDR compliance in Europe. Channel Expansion: RIA net flows of $9 billion (41% of total), via partnerships with LPL Financial and Commonwealth, where our SMAs now represent 12% of their model portfolios. Institutional wins included a $2.5 billion carve-out from a BlackRock balanced mandate, citing our superior downside protection in 2022's drawdown. Regional Momentum: Americas contributed 65% of NNA ($14.3B), APAC 22% ($4.8B) from Middle East family offices diversifying into our infrastructure debt fund (yielding 8.2% net), and EMEA 13% ($2.9B), rebounding post-Brexit with DB pension consolidations.

Challenges persist: Competition from Vanguard's zero-fee ETFs eroded some core fixed income flows, but our active fixed income book grew 11% on duration positioning ahead of rate cuts.

Looking ahead, we're doubling down on "retention-plus" strategies: Investing $150 million in GenAI for hyper-personalized advice, targeting 98% retention by FY2026. We'll accelerate alternatives ramp-up—aiming for 25% of AUM from today's 18%—with a new evergreen PE fund closing $10 billion by year-end. Regionally, APAC is our growth engine, with a Singapore hub hiring 50 staff for $50 billion AUM target in five years. Risks include regulatory tailwinds like DOL fiduciary rules favoring active RIAs, but we're stress-testing for recessionary redemptions.

In summary, our client franchise is firing on all cylinders, positioning GAP for 10-12% organic NNA growth in FY2025.

Thank you, Sarah. Before I hand it back for Q&A, I want to spend a few minutes on our capital allocation strategy, which remains a cornerstone of delivering long-term shareholder value at Global Asset Partners, or what we affectionately call GAP. In an industry where assets under management—or AUM—have grown to $1.2 trillion globally amid choppy markets, our disciplined approach has enabled us to navigate higher-for-longer interest rates, persistent inflation, and the great rotation from growth to value stocks. We've generated $2.8 billion in fee-related earnings over the past 12 months, up 8% year-over-year, providing ample dry powder for opportunistic deployment.

Let me break this down into our four-pillar framework: shareholder returns, organic growth investments, inorganic M&A, and technology and infrastructure. This isn't just a checklist—it's a dynamic playbook informed by our proprietary capital allocation scorecard, which weighs ROIC targets above 15%, IRR hurdles for new initiatives at 20%+, and alignment with our three strategic pillars: scaling passive and ETF franchises, expanding alternatives like private credit and infrastructure, and deepening ESG integration.

First, shareholder returns. We've maintained a progressive dividend policy with a target payout ratio of 45-50% of adjusted operating earnings, reflecting our confidence in sticky fee streams from our $450 billion core long-only equity and fixed income mandates. In Q3 alone, we declared a quarterly dividend of $0.42 per share, a 7% increase from last year, yielding approximately 2.8% based on current trading levels—competitive with peers like T. Rowe Price but with superior growth prospects. Complementing this, our board authorized a $1.5 billion share repurchase program in July, of which we've executed $900 million to date at an average price 12% below our estimated NAV per share. This opportunistic buyback—prioritizing when our stock trades at a 10-15% discount to tangible book value—has accreted $0.25 to EPS YTD. Amid the 2024 market volatility, with the S&P 500 up 18% but small-cap lagging, we've been net buyers, reducing shares outstanding by 2.1%.

Second, organic growth. Here, we're laser-focused on high-conviction product launches and seeding to capture structural tailwinds. We've committed $3.2 billion in seed capital over the last two years to 15 new strategies, including our flagship GAP Sustainable Equity ETF suite, which has amassed $12 billion in AUM since inception in 2022—outpacing BlackRock's iShares ESG Aware series in flows per the Morningstar data. In alternatives, we've seeded $1.1 billion into private credit funds targeting 9-11% net IRRs in a 5%+ SOFR environment, where dry powder across the industry sits at $1.7 trillion per Preqin. Regionally, we're tilting toward APAC, where we've launched three UCITS-compliant strategies domiciled in Luxembourg, drawing $4.5 billion in net new money from sovereign wealth funds like GIC and Temasek. This contrasts with Europe, where MiFID II headwinds have slowed active equity flows; there, we're pivoting to model portfolios and SMAs, growing that book to $80 billion, up 22% YoY.

Third, inorganic M&A. Discipline reigns supreme—we target 3-5 deals annually with strict accretion thresholds: EPS accretive in Year 1, 15%+ ROIC by Year 3. Our $2.4 billion acquisition of boutique fixed income manager Horizon Capital in Q1 exemplifies this: it added $65 billion in AUM at a 4.5% fee rate, immediately boosting our fee-related revenue mix to 72%. We're emulating Blackstone's playbook in alternatives but with a multi-strategy focus, including a pending $800 million tuck-in for a London-based infrastructure debt platform amid the U.K.'s £50 billion National Wealth Fund initiative. In the U.S., we've passed on frothy valuations—multiples at 12-14x fee-related earnings versus our 10x trading discount—but our pipeline remains robust at $15 billion across 20 opportunities, skewed 60% to alternatives boutiques and 40% to tech-enabled distribution platforms.

Finally, technology and infrastructure. We're investing $450 million annually—up 15% from 2023—in our next-gen "GAP Alpha" platform, a cloud-native Aladdin competitor leveraging generative AI for alpha generation and risk analytics. This includes $150 million in machine learning models for dynamic asset allocation, reducing model risk by 30% in backtests across 2022's rate shock. We've also deployed $100 million in distribution tech, including API integrations with platforms like Addepar and Envestnet, driving a 25% uptick in RIA channel flows. Balance sheet-wise, we're fortress-like: net debt to EBITDA at 1.2x, $5.2 billion in liquidity, and undrawn revolvers. No material maturities until 2028.

Looking forward, amid Fed projections for 75bps of cuts in 2025 and EM growth at 4.2% per IMF, we'll maintain this framework with a 60/40 split between returns and growth investments. We're committing 20% of incremental free cash flow to buybacks if our discount persists, while ramping alternatives to 25% of AUM by 2026—targeting the $18 trillion private markets opportunity as defined by McKinsey.
